name: Foundry Virtual Tabletop
tagline: Self-hosted virtual tabletop for running tabletop RPGs online, with maps, tokens, dynamic lighting, dice and a huge module ecosystem.

pricing.basis: one-time license per host, players join free
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The unglamorous core of a virtual tabletop is a shared image, some draggable tokens on a grid, a dice roller and a chat log, and a coding agent can absolutely stand that up over a weekend. What it will not reproduce is the part people actually pay for: dynamic vision with walls and light sources, the game system layers that encode entire rulesets into character sheets and automated rolls, and roughly a thousand community modules that fix or extend everything else. Foundry is also already self-hosted with a one-time license, so you are not escaping a subscription, you are escaping a modest one-off cost by rebuilding ten years of someone else's canvas engineering. If your table owns physical books and rolls its own math, the DIY version is genuinely fine. If you run a heavily automated Pathfinder 2e campaign, do not.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted room where a GM uploads a map, players drag tokens on a snapped grid in realtime, reveal fog with a brush, and roll dice into a shared chat log.
requirements: Node 20+ and a machine or small VPS that can stay online during sessions
Your own map images and token art
A tunnel or port forward so players outside your LAN can connect
Players willing to look up their own rules
whatYouLose: Dynamic lighting, wall occlusion and per-token vision, which is the single hardest thing to fake
Game system packages: full character sheets, ruleset automation, compendiums of spells, monsters and items
The module ecosystem, where someone has already solved the annoying thing you are about to hit
Officially licensed content packs and premium adventure modules
Polished session logistics: audio playlists, scene transitions, journal handouts, player permissions, combat trackers that actually work
moatNotes: The license is cheap; the module and game-system community around it is the product. A clone starts with an empty registry.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because it is a one-time cost that buys a decade of canvas rendering work plus a community that has already automated your specific ruleset. Most groups do not want a shared whiteboard, they want the D&D 5e sheet that rolls attacks correctly, the vision system that hides the corridor, and the module that adds weather. Rebuilding the shared whiteboard is a fun weekend. Rebuilding the ecosystem is a career.
notes: A DIY map-and-dice room is legitimately usable for rules-light play; the moment your table wants automated character sheets, buy the license.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted virtual tabletop for a small tabletop RPG group. Empty folder, no scaffolding tools.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Node 20, Express, Socket.IO for realtime
- Vanilla JS client with PixiJS for the map canvas
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for persistence
- No build step, serve static files directly

Features, in scope:
- One shared session. On load, ask for a display name and a room password checked against ROOM_PASSWORD in .env. One name matching GM_NAME in .env gets GM powers.
- GM uploads a map image (multipart, stored in ./uploads). GM sets grid size in pixels and toggles grid display.
- Tokens: GM can add a token from an uploaded image, set its name, size in grid squares, and owner name. Owners and the GM can drag their tokens; drags snap to grid and broadcast to everyone over Socket.IO with optimistic local movement.
- Fog of war: a black mask layer over the map. GM paints reveals with a circular brush; revealed regions persist and are visible to all players. GM can reset fog.
- Dice roller: a chat input that parses standard notation like 2d6+3 and 1d20-1, rolls server side, and posts the individual dice plus total into a shared chat log. Plain text messages also go to the log. GM can send whispers to one player.
- Initiative tracker: ordered list of names with numbers, GM editable, visible to all, with a next-turn button that highlights the active entry.
- Ping: any player alt-clicks the map to show a brief animated marker for everyone.
- Everything persists across restarts: map, grid, tokens, fog mask, chat log, initiative.

Out of scope, do not build:
- Dynamic lighting, walls, line of sight, or per-token vision
- Character sheets, rulesets, compendiums, or any game system logic
- Accounts, email, billing, telemetry, or any third-party API
- Mobile-specific UI, though the canvas should tolerate a tablet

Deliver: server.js, public/ with index.html plus client JS, a schema created on first run, .env.example listing ROOM_PASSWORD and GM_NAME and PORT, and a README with run instructions and one paragraph on exposing the port to players safely. Keep dependencies minimal and comment the socket event contract at the top of server.js.
